explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus says, "If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first." He puts His own name at the front of the line. The disciples aren't hearing about something that skipped over Him.

John the Baptist is the man who baptized Jesus (Matthew 3:13-17), so I get why his name floated up. But Jesus doesn't mention him here. He says the world hated Him first: "If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first." Jesus is the answer.
Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, and it's a fair guess. But he's not in this verse at all. Jesus says, "If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first." He's talking about Himself.
Yes, love. Jesus says, "If you were of the world, it would love you as its own." Then He says the world hates them instead, because they are not of the world. He has chosen them out of it.
Ignore sounds mild, and I wish it were that mild. But Jesus says the world would love them as its own if they were of the world. Instead, He says, the world hates them. The word He uses is love.

Fear is a big word, and it didn't make the verse. Jesus says, "If you were of the world, it would love you as its own." That's the word that goes in the blank. Then comes the turn: the world hates them because they are not of the world.

That's what He says. "If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well." Jesus just lined it up straight, no sugar on top. He isn't springing it on them later, either. He's telling them tonight, up front.

I'd love for that to be the answer, friend. But Jesus says, "If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well." The same treatment He got is coming for them. Peace isn't what He promises in this verse.

Forgotten would almost be a break. But Jesus says, "If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well." These people aren't forgetting anybody. They're going to treat the disciples the way they treated Jesus.

True! Jesus says it right after the persecution line: "if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well." He doesn't leave the disciples with only the heavy half. Their word will be kept by some, just like His was.
This one is true, baker. Jesus says, "if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well." It sits right next to the line about persecution. He gives both halves, and the second half is easy to miss.

That's it. Jesus says they will treat the disciples like this "because of My name, since they do not know the One who sent Me." The trouble is tied to His name and to not knowing the One who sent Him. That's what He tells them.
That man is John the Baptist (Matthew 3:13-17), and he doesn't show up in this verse. Jesus says they do not know "the One who sent Me." Keep your eyes on that phrase.

Good thinking, since the disciples are the ones getting treated this way. But Jesus doesn't say that these people don't know the followers. He says they do not know "the One who sent Me." The answer is the One who sent Jesus.
Jesus says the opposite. He says, "Now, however, they have no excuse for their sin." He had come and spoken to them, so the excuse is gone. It's a serious line, so I'll keep my jokes in the oven.

Right, it's false. Jesus says, "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not be guilty of sin." Then He says, "Now, however, they have no excuse for their sin." He did come, and He did speak. It's a heavy line, friend.
Yes! Jesus says, "Whoever hates Me hates My Father as well." It's one short line. The hatred doesn't stop at Jesus, and He says so plainly.
Moses was Israel's leader, so I see why he came to mind. But Jesus doesn't name him here. He says, "Whoever hates Me hates My Father as well." The answer is His Father.

Abraham is the man God called to leave his homeland (Genesis 12:1), and he's a fine name to reach for. But he isn't in this verse. Jesus says, "Whoever hates Me hates My Father as well." His Father is the one He names.
Jesus says they did see. His words are, "now they have seen and hated both Me and My Father." They saw the works, and they hated both Him and His Father. So the line is false.

That's right, it's false. Jesus says He did works among them that no one else did, and that "now they have seen and hated both Me and My Father." They saw the works. It's the hatred that's the heavy part.
Careful, friend, because it's the reverse. Jesus quotes the line as "They hated Me without reason." Without reason means no good reason. So the line is false.
Yes, it's false. Jesus says the line written in their Law is, "They hated Me without reason." There's no good reason in it. He says this hatred fulfills what is written.
Yes! Jesus says the Advocate, the Spirit of truth, "will testify about Me." The Advocate comes from the Father, and Jesus says He will send Him. That's the hope I was hollering about, friend.
Fighting is a fair guess when trouble is on the way. But that isn't what Jesus says the Advocate does here. He says, "He will testify about Me." Testifying is the answer.

explanations.answer: Take them out of the world
explanations.explanation: Jesus actually says something different. He has chosen the disciples out of the world (John 15:19), but He doesn't say the Advocate takes them out. He says the Advocate "will testify about Me." That's the job He names.

True. Jesus says, "And you also must testify, because you have been with Me from the beginning." The Advocate testifies, and so do the disciples. They've been with Jesus from the beginning, and He gives that as the reason.

It's true, baker. Jesus says, "And you also must testify, because you have been with Me from the beginning." The Advocate testifies about Him, and so do the disciples. Jesus gives their time with Him as the reason.

explanations.answer: So they will not fall away
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, "I have told you these things so that you will not fall away." He isn't scaring them for fun. He's telling them ahead of time, and that's the purpose He gives.
That's not the reason He gives, friend. Jesus says, "I have told you these things so that you will not fall away." Fighting back isn't in the verse. Not falling away is.

explanations.answer: So they will hide from the world
explanations.explanation: Hiding isn't what He says. Jesus says, "I have told you these things so that you will not fall away." That's the reason He gives. The verse doesn't mention hiding at all.
Yes. Jesus says, "a time is coming when anyone who kills you will think he is offering a service to God." The word that matters is think. This is a heavy line, and Jesus says it plainly.
Jesus doesn't say anything about a city here. He says the person "will think he is offering a service to God." That's the answer. It's a heavy one.

Rome was the empire that ruled the land back then, so I see the thought. But it isn't in this verse. Jesus says anyone who kills them "will think he is offering a service to God." That's what He says, and it's a heavy thing to hear.

Yes, remember. Jesus says, "I have told you these things so that when their hour comes, you will remember that I told you about them." He's telling them early. That way, when the hour comes, they'll remember He said it.
Doubt isn't the word, baker. Jesus says they will "remember that I told you about them." He tells them early so that when their hour comes, they'll remember He told them.

It's the opposite. Jesus says, "I have told you these things so that when their hour comes, you will remember that I told you about them." Telling them ahead of time is how they'll remember. Remember goes in the blank.
Jesus says otherwise. His words are, "I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you." He's telling them now, on this night. So the line is false.
Yes, it's false. Jesus says, "I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you." He's saying it now, at this supper. The text gives that reason, so I don't have to guess.
